The delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, today and members of the House, I want to speak my point of personal privilege. I'd like to honor the legacy of black midwives who carried life through some of the darkest moments in American history.

Midwives, as well as doulas, hold a very special place in my heart. Midwifery among African Americans were female-dominated family profession. Knowledge was sacred. It was passed down from mother to daughter, from grandmother to granddaughter.

It was more than a skill. It was a calling. It combined medical knowledge, herbal remedies, spiritual practices, and deep community trust. In many ways, midwifery and spirituality were one and the same.

Now, during slavery, African-American midwives were essential members of their communities. Though enslaved themselves, they held their respective positions among enslaved people. They were healers. They were caretakers. They were counselors, and they were protectors of life.

Slave owners relied on these women. They used these medical professionals to ensure health of enslaved women who were forced to reproduce. Healthy births meant expanding the labor force. Enslaved women's bodies were treated as property.

And midwives were expected to safeguard that slaveholders saw as economic investment. Newborn infants will one day become a part of the labor pool. So these midwives not only delivered the babies for the slave woman and perhaps her husband, but she was also delivering the babies that were fathered by the slaveholders.
Throughout this rural and remote parts of the South, African-American midwives served both black and white women. These women delivered generations into this world.

They reduced infant mortality. They provided comfort, safety, and dignity in childbirth. They were pillars of the community. Despite later efforts in the early 20th century to discredit and push midwives out of the practice through medical licensing laws and racial bias, their impact cannot be erased.

the legacy of black midwives lives on. They live on in the life of Claudine Curry-Smith. She was a prominent African-American midwife and a community figure from Northern Neck region of Virginia, specifically Lancaster County.

Her career spanned more than three decades when she delivered more than 500 babies. Despite the practicing in homes that were often without running water or electricity, she never lost a mother in her care.

I hope that you agree that the midwife's knowledge, resilience, and spiritual grounding continue to inspire those who carry this sacred work forward today. Every modern midwife, every birth worker who centers compassion, culture, and community stands on the shoulders of these women that came before them. Black midwives during slavery were more than just attendants at birth. They were guardians of life in a system built on dehumanization. They preserved

African traditions of healing. They embodied strength, wisdom, and quiet resistance. They were healers in a system that denied their humanity. Their hands caught more than just babies. They carried hope. Their legacy lives on in every midwife who honors ancestral knowledge, community care, and the sacredness of life. So during this month, Black History Month, please remember the legacy of black midwives during slavery and beyond. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

The Delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Today marks the beginning of Lunar New Year, a holiday celebrated by Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, Mongolian, Tibetan, and many Southeast Asian communities to welcome the spring season and a new beginning.

The Lunar New Year is filled with familiar symbols, red for luck and joy, the lion dance, firecrackers, and the 12-year cycle of animals. Today, we enter the year of the horse, a year associated with energy, freedom, and bold action.

You'll notice on your desk small hanging ornaments with symbols of good fortune offered as we welcome the new year together. For thousands of years, Lunar New Year has reminded us of the importance of family, the power of renewal, and the promise that each year brings new beginnings.

It also teaches us that just as the moon moves through its phases, our lives, both personal and collective, move through the cycles of growth, struggle, and change. In that spirit, we pause to honor those who came before us.

In 1587, in the year of the pig, Filipino sailors crossed the Pacific and set foot on this land, becoming the first recorded Asians to arrive in what would one day become the United States. decades before Jamestown. From the very beginning, our presence has been a part of America's story.

History, like the lunar calendar, does not move in straight lines. In the year of the snake in 1869, Chinese immigrants laid steel across mountains to complete the transcontinental railroad, even as they were denied belonging. In the year of the horse in 1882, their exclusion was written into law. And again, in the year of the horse, 1942, Japanese-American families were imprisoned behind barbed wire, not for what they had done, but for who they were. Even in those years,

change still came. In the year of the sheep, 1943, exclusion was repealed. In the year of the dog, in 1946, Filipino and Indian immigrants were allowed to claim citizenship. In the year of the in 1965, America dismantled race-based immigration quotas. In the Year of the Monkey in 1980, the Refugee Act affirmed compassion as national policy. And in the Year of the Dog in 1982, the killing of Vincent Chin transformed grief into a civil rights movement that refused invisibility. Here in Virginia, that arc

bent closer to representation. In the Year of the Ox in 2009, former delegate Mark King became the first Korean American and Asian-born immigrant elected to state government. In the year of the rooster in 2017, our own delegate Cathy Tran became the first Vietnamese American elected to the General Assembly. And in the year of the tiger in 2022, our own delegate Irene Shin became the first Korean American woman elected, expanding who could see themselves reflected in these halls. And so today, in the year of the horse, in the oldest continuously

operating lawmaking body in the Western Hemisphere, I stand here humbled as the first Chinese American ever elected to state government in the Commonwealth, not as an ending, but as a continuation of their progress. This is not my achievement alone, but the result of generations who endured hardship, built community, and believed their children could stand where they could not.

Moments like these invite us not to only reflect on how far we've come, but to look ahead to what comes next. The Spring Festival is a time to hope. The horse calls us to move forward with courage. I believe we can rise to that call. Building on a fairer economy, safer communities, stronger schools, broader access to care and a more inclusive Commonwealth. After a long winter, people gather, celebrate and begin again. Let us all share goodwill, extend happiness and step into to the new year together.
Happy New Year, wishing you all prosperity.
